title: Paper from Samarkand
hookLine: papermaking spreads west, and books become cheaper

lines: ONCE, EVERY PAGE HAD A PRICE.
cards: A receipt. A sticky note. A shopping list on the back of an envelope.
Paper is so ordinary now that it gets thrown away by the handful.
Yet for a long time, writing something down meant writing on something costly: the scraped and dried skin of an animal, or papyrus reeds that grew along the Nile. Every page had a price.
All those translations in Baghdad needed something to be written on. The answer came from the east, by way of a city on the Silk Road called Samarkand. Today: warraqun, the paper people.

teach.b: Paper came from China, made from plant fibers and rags beaten into pulp, spread thin on a screen, and dried.

Later writers tell a story about how it reached the Muslim world: after a battle in Central Asia, Chinese prisoners were brought to Samarkand, and some of them knew how to make paper and taught the craft there.
It's a good story. Historians question it, and some think the knowledge traveled more slowly, along trade routes.
Either way, Samarkand paper became known, and before long paper was being made in Baghdad too.
The historian Ibn Khaldun says that the Barmakid minister al-Fadl ibn Yahya, from the family in Harun's story, had government records written on paper. Now see what that did.
Paper was cheaper than skin and easier to come by than papyrus. Cheaper paper meant cheaper books. Baghdad grew a market of booksellers and copyists, called warraqun, the paper people.

The bookseller Ibn al-Nadim, whose catalog told of al-Ma'mun's dream, was one of them. Scholars could own more books, students could copy their teachers' lectures, and the translations of the House of Wisdom could travel.
The Qur'an speaks of God, in Pickthall's words, "Who teacheth by the pen." A pen needs a page. In this story, the page got cheap, and learning spread.

how: Historians of the book study surviving paper manuscripts from the Muslim world, and calligraphers today still prepare paper by hand for copying the Qur'an and other texts.

practice: Hold a sheet of paper for a moment, feeling how thin and light it is, and bring to mind the long chain behind it: the craft carried from China, the mills of Samarkand and Baghdad, the copyists in their market.

Then write one line by hand, slowly, something you're grateful for or something you've learned. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah, as some Muslims do before writing; if not, just write with care.

wordCard.voice: Warraqun, the paper people: the booksellers and copyists who multiplied once paper reached Baghdad by way of Samarkand, making books cheaper and learning easier to share. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: leaves or sheets, the word used for paper; the warraq was the paper person, copyist and bookseller.
